title: Somalia Deyr floods — 2023
brief_outcome_free: South-central Somalia (Shabelle basin), Deyr season. Riverine and flash flooding along the Shabelle; displacement risk. You are the DOC duty analyst as the forecast window opens.

peak.description: Flood onset / peak — see the Risk Knowledge storyline for the recorded loss & damage.

rounds.title: Early monitoring (2023-09-18)
rounds.engine_state: Antecedent moisture building; ensemble exceedance still modest

rounds.title: Forecast escalation (2023-09-23)

evidence_cards.label: Ensemble-mean exceedance prob (ECMWF P_heavy)
evidence_cards.source: ECMWF ensemble P(any member >= 2-yr RP), mean
evidence_cards.teaching_note: The ensemble MEAN can look benign for convective floods. Watch the tail.

evidence_cards.label: Ensemble-max / 2-yr RP (pixel p95)
evidence_cards.teaching_note: Only the tail fires for many flash floods — the signal a mean-threshold system misses.

evidence_cards.label: Yesterday's posterior carried forward (DBN, alpha=0.6)
evidence_cards.teaching_note: Temporal coupling = virtual evidence; keeps the signal elevated near onset.

act1_quiz.prompt: As the 2023 Deyr season opens over south-central Somalia, which combination of large-scale climate drivers is loading the season toward enhanced rainfall?
act1_quiz.hint: Both the Pacific and the Indian Ocean are in anomalous states in late 2023.
options: La Nina with a negative Indian Ocean Dipole
A strong El Nino together with a strongly positive Indian Ocean Dipole
A neutral Pacific with no Indian Ocean signal
act1_quiz.correct: A strong El Nino together with a strongly positive Indian Ocean Dipole
act1_quiz.answer_note: By the start of Deyr 2023 a strong El Nino was established in the Pacific and the Indian Ocean Dipole was strongly positive, warming the western Indian Ocean. Both drivers historically enhance the October-December rains over the Horn of Africa, so the prior on heavy Deyr rainfall is elevated before any single storm is forecast.
act1_quiz.bn_purpose: How known seasonal climate drivers raise the baseline flood prior before short-range forecast evidence arrives.

act1_quiz.prompt: Lower Shabelle's riverine villages can flood even when local rainfall over Somalia is moderate. Why?
act1_quiz.hint: Follow the Shabelle upstream on a map.
options: The Shabelle is tidal, so the ocean pushes water upstream
Much of the Shabelle's flow is generated by rain over the upstream Ethiopian highlands, which travels downstream into Somalia days later
Local irrigation canals are the only flood source
Riverine flooding in Somalia only happens during the Gu season
act1_quiz.correct: Much of the Shabelle's flow is generated by rain over the upstream Ethiopian highlands, which travels downstream into Somalia days later
act1_quiz.answer_note: The Shabelle basin extends deep into the Ethiopian highlands, so heavy rain there raises river levels in Somalia with a lag of days. A duty analyst must therefore watch upstream catchment rainfall and river gauges, not just the local forecast, and the lag also offers usable warning lead time.
act1_quiz.bn_purpose: Why upstream catchment evidence matters as much as local rainfall for riverine flood reasoning.

decision.checkpoint_prompt: The ensemble mean may look benign but the tail signal is rising ahead of onset. What DOC level do you set, and why? A 'Watch + re-check + note the tail uncertainty' is a strong answer.

counterfactual.prompt: What if a precautionary no-regret action (pre-position relief, alert riverine villages and ready evacuation) were taken at the lead round on the tail signal?
counterfactual.narrative: Acting on a short-lead tail signal is exactly what the flood BN's tail_risk node exists to surface. The counterfactual illustrates loss reduction without claiming certainty.
